source.text: וַֽיִּשְׁבְּת֡וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת הָאֲנָשִׁ֣ים הָ֭אֵלֶּה מֵעֲנ֣וֹת אֶת־אִיּ֑וֹב כִּ֤י ה֖וּא צַדִּ֣יק בְּעֵינָֽיו׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And ceased the three men the these from answering Job, for he [was] righteous in his eyes.

en.L: And these three men ceased answering Job, because he [was] righteous in his [own] eyes.
en.B: So these three men stopped answering Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
en.R: So Job's three friends stopped arguing with him, because Job was sure that he was in the right.

decisions.choice: these three men: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar; the debate with them is over
decisions.reason: The three friends came in 2:11 and have spoken in turn since chapter 4. Bildad's last speech was short (chapter 25) and Zophar does not speak a third time, so the debate runs down. Verses 1-5 are prose, the first narrative since chapter 2; they bring in a new speaker, Elihu, before his speeches in poetry begin (32:6b-37:24).

decisions.choice: righteous in his own eyes: he was sure that he was in the right
decisions.reason: "In his own eyes" means in his own judgment (Proverbs 3:7; 26:12). Job had held fast to his innocence to the end (27:5-6; chapter 31), so the friends gave up trying to convince him. The narrator reports how things stood between them; the phrase does not itself say whether Job was right.

decisions.choice: in his eyes, as the Hebrew has it
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek and Syriac translations read "in their eyes": the friends could no longer answer because Job seemed righteous to them. The Hebrew text, followed here, says "in his eyes": Job considered himself righteous.

decisions.choice: Job's three friends; stopped arguing with him; sure that he was in the right (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable names the three men as Job's friends and says plainly what "answering" and "righteous in his own eyes" mean here (m1, m2).

source.text: וַיִּ֤חַר אַ֨ף׀אֱלִיה֣וּא בֶן־בַּרַכְאֵ֣ל הַבּוּזִי֮ מִמִּשְׁפַּ֪חַ֫ת רָ֥ם בְּ֭אִיּוֹב חָרָ֣ה אַפּ֑וֹ עַֽל־צַדְּק֥וֹ נַ֝פְשׁ֗וֹ מֵאֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And burned [the] anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, from [the] clan of Ram; against Job burned his anger, because he justified himself more than God.

en.L: Then the anger of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the clan of Ram, burned; against Job his anger burned, because he justified himself rather than God.
en.B: Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the clan of Ram, became angry. He was angry with Job because Job made himself out to be in the right rather than God.
en.R: Then Elihu became very angry. He was the son of Barachel the Buzite, from the family of Ram. He was angry with Job because Job said that he himself was right and God was wrong.

decisions.choice: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the clan of Ram: a new speaker, given a full family line
decisions.reason: Elihu has not been mentioned before and is not named again after chapter 37: he is not among the friends of 2:11 or 42:7-9. His name means "He is my God". Buz was a son of Nahor and brother of Uz (Genesis 22:21), and a people of the desert named with Dedan and Tema (Jeremiah 25:23), so he comes from the same eastern world as Job, whose home is Uz (1:1). The clan of Ram is otherwise unknown. Unlike the friends, he is given a father and a clan, as a young man is introduced.

decisions.choice: his anger burned: he became angry
decisions.reason: Hebrew says that anger, literally the nose, burns or grows hot. The phrase comes four times in verses 2-5: against Job (twice), against the friends (verse 3) and once more in verse 5. The repetition shows the force of feeling behind Elihu's speech.

decisions.choice: justified himself rather than God: claimed to be in the right at God's expense
decisions.reason: The word "from" (min) here compares: Job held himself to be in the right more than God, that is, by insisting he was innocent he made God out to be in the wrong. God puts the same charge to Job in 40:8: "Will you condemn me so that you may be in the right?" The word can also mean "before God" (as 4:17), but Elihu's anger points to the comparison.

decisions.choice: became angry; made himself out to be in the right (Balanced); said that he himself was right and God was wrong (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "became angry" for the burning of anger (m2), name Job where "he" could be unclear, and spell out what "justified himself rather than God" means (m3). Readable splits the long sentence and states the comparison plainly.

source.text: וּבִשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת רֵעָיו֮ חָרָ֪ה אַ֫פּ֥וֹ עַ֤ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־מָצְא֣וּ מַעֲנֶ֑ה וַ֝יַּרְשִׁ֗יעוּ אֶת־אִיּֽוֹב׃

records.literal_gloss: And against [the] three of his companions burned his anger, because that not they had found an answer, and they condemned Job.

en.L: And against his three friends his anger burned, because they had not found an answer, and [yet] had condemned Job.
en.B: He was also angry with his three friends, because they had found no answer, and yet they had declared Job guilty.
en.R: He was also angry with Job's three friends. They had not found any answer to what Job said, but they still said that Job was guilty.

decisions.choice: condemned: declared guilty
decisions.reason: The verb (rasha' in the causative) is a law-court word: to declare someone guilty, the opposite of declaring someone in the right (Deuteronomy 25:1; Job 9:20; 10:2). The friends had judged Job a wrongdoer without being able to answer his case.

decisions.choice: and: here "and yet"
decisions.reason: The two clauses stand side by side with a simple "and", but the second is the opposite of what the first would lead one to expect: having no answer, they still condemned him. That is why Elihu is angry with them.

decisions.choice: condemned Job, as the Hebrew text has it
decisions.reason: Jewish scribal tradition lists this verse among the "corrections of the scribes", places where the text is said to have been changed out of reverence for God. On that account the verse once read that the friends "condemned God": by failing to answer Job, they made God appear in the wrong. The tradition cannot be checked against any surviving manuscript, and the text as it stands, "Job", makes good sense, so it is followed here.

decisions.choice: any answer to what Job said (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear what the friends could not answer: Job's words.

source.text: וֶֽאֱלִיה֗וּ חִכָּ֣ה אֶת־אִ֭יּוֹב בִּדְבָרִ֑ים כִּ֤י זְֽקֵנִים־הֵ֖מָּה מִמֶּ֣נּוּ לְיָמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And Elihu had waited [for] Job with words, for older they [were] than he in days.

en.L: Now Elihu had waited [to speak] to Job with words, because they [were] older than he in days.
en.B: Elihu had waited before speaking to Job, because the others were older than he was.
en.R: Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he was.

decisions.choice: had waited with words for Job: held back his own words while the others spoke to Job
alternatives: had waited while Job was speaking
decisions.reason: The verb means to wait patiently (Isaiah 30:18). With "with words" it most likely means that Elihu waited to address Job until the others had finished; it could also mean that he waited through Job's words. Verses 11-12 say he listened to the whole debate.

decisions.choice: older than he: the old speak first
decisions.reason: In the ancient East the aged were expected to speak first and the young to listen (15:10; 29:8). Elihu explains his silence in the same terms in verses 6-7.

decisions.choice: the others (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "They" means the three friends and Job; Balanced and Readable say "the others" so that the pronoun is not taken to mean Job alone.

source.text: וַיַּ֤רְא אֱלִיה֗וּא כִּ֘י אֵ֤ין מַעֲנֶ֗ה בְּ֭פִי שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת הָאֲנָשִׁ֗ים וַיִּ֥חַר אַפּֽוֹ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And saw Elihu that there was no answer in [the] mouth of [the] three the men, and burned his anger.

en.L: And Elihu saw that there [was] no answer in the mouth of the three men, and his anger burned.
en.B: When Elihu saw that the three men had no answer left, he became angry.
en.R: When Elihu saw that the three men had nothing more to say, he became angry.

decisions.choice: no answer in their mouth: they had nothing more to say
decisions.reason: The mouth stands for speech. The friends had run out of replies to Job (verse 3). Elihu's anger, already named in verses 2-3, is said once more to explain why he now breaks in.

decisions.choice: became angry (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, Balanced and Readable use the plain English for the Hebrew picture of burning anger.

source.text: וַיַּ֤עַן׀אֱלִיה֖וּא בֶן־בַּֽרַכְאֵ֥ל הַבּוּזִ֗י וַיֹּ֫אמַ֥ר צָ֘עִ֤יר אֲנִ֣י לְ֭יָמִים וְאַתֶּ֣ם יְשִׁישִׁ֑ים עַל־כֵּ֖ן זָחַ֥לְתִּי וָֽאִירָ֓א׀מֵחַוֺּ֖ת דֵּעִ֣י אֶתְכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite and said: Young I [am] in days, and you [are] aged; therefore I shrank back and I was afraid from declaring my knowledge [to] you.

en.L: And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: \q I [am] young in days, and you [are] aged; \q therefore I shrank back and was afraid \q to declare my knowledge to you.
en.B: Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered: \q I am young in years, and you are old; \q so I held back and was afraid \q to tell you what I know.
en.R: Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite said: \q I am young, and you are old. \q So I was shy and afraid \q to tell you what I think.

decisions.choice: Elihu answered and said: the start of his speeches, which run to 37:24
decisions.reason: The introduction follows the pattern of the other speakers (4:1; 8:1; 11:1). From here Elihu speaks in poetry; the introduction is the verse's first line, as a psalm's title can be. His speeches are introduced at 32:6, 34:1, 35:1 and 36:1, and no one answers him.

decisions.choice: shrank back: was timid, held back in fear
decisions.reason: The verb (zachal) is rare. Its other use describes things that crawl in the dust (Deuteronomy 32:24), so here it pictures the young man drawing back, too timid to come forward.

decisions.choice: my knowledge: what I know, my view
decisions.reason: The word for knowledge here (dea') is used in the Bible only by Elihu (32:6, 10, 17; 36:3; 37:16). It is what he knows and has to say, his view of the matter.

decisions.choice: answered (Balanced); said (Readable)
decisions.reason: Speech introductions in Job follow one pattern: Literal "answered and said", Balanced "answered", Readable "said" (as 4:1).

decisions.choice: shy; what I think (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for the young man's timidity and for his "knowledge", which here is his view of the matter (m3).

source.text: אָ֭מַרְתִּי יָמִ֣ים יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ וְרֹ֥ב שָׁ֝נִ֗ים יֹדִ֥יעוּ חָכְמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: I said, days should speak, and abundance of years should make known wisdom.

en.L: I said, Days should speak, \q and [the] abundance of years should make wisdom known.
en.B: I thought, Let age speak, \q and let those with many years teach wisdom.
en.R: I thought, Let the older people speak. \q People who have lived many years should teach wisdom.

decisions.choice: days, many years: those who are old
decisions.reason: Elihu speaks of age as if it were a person: "days" and "many years" stand for the old men who have lived them. It was a common belief that wisdom comes with age (12:12; 15:10), which Elihu now questions (verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: I said: I said to myself, I thought
decisions.reason: "I said" often means "I thought" in Hebrew (Psalm 30:7; 31:23). Elihu describes what he had been thinking while he waited.

decisions.choice: I thought; age (Balanced); the older people (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "I thought" (m2), and turn "days" into "age" or "the older people" (m1).

source.text: אָ֭כֵן רֽוּחַ־הִ֣יא בֶאֱנ֑וֹשׁ וְנִשְׁמַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י תְּבִינֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: But truly, [the] spirit it [is] in a mortal, and [the] breath of [the] Almighty gives them understanding.

en.L: But truly, it [is the] spirit in a mortal, \q and [the] breath of the Almighty [that] gives them understanding.
en.B: But it is the spirit in a person, \q the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding.
en.R: But it is the spirit in people, \q the breath of God All-Powerful, that makes them understand.

decisions.choice: the spirit: the life and mind that God breathes into human beings
alternatives: the Spirit of God in a person
decisions.reason: The word (ruach) means wind, breath or spirit. Here it stands beside "the breath of the Almighty", the breath God breathed into the first human (Genesis 2:7), as in 27:3 and 33:4. Elihu says that understanding comes from this God-given spirit, not from age. It may refer to God's own Spirit at work in a person, as Pharaoh said of Joseph (Genesis 41:38); lowercase "spirit" keeps the line's focus on the spirit as it is in a human being, while the parallel makes clear that it comes from God.

decisions.choice: but truly: a contrast with what Elihu had thought (verse 7)
decisions.reason: The word ('akhen) marks a realization that overturns an earlier view: "but in fact" (Isaiah 53:4; Psalm 31:23). Elihu had expected the old to speak wisely; now he sees that wisdom is God's gift.

decisions.choice: the Almighty: Shaddai
decisions.reason: Shaddai, an ancient name of God, is rendered "the Almighty" (see 5:17).

decisions.choice: a mortal: any human being
decisions.reason: The word ('enosh) means a human being, frail and mortal, men and women alike (as 4:17; 9:2). The pronoun "them" in the second line refers to human beings in general.

decisions.choice: the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The two halves of the verse name one thing from two sides; Balanced and Readable join them into one statement, with the breath of the Almighty in apposition to the spirit.

decisions.choice: God All-Powerful (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says "God All-Powerful" for Shaddai in every book.

source.text: לֹֽא־רַבִּ֥ים יֶחְכָּ֑מוּ וּ֝זְקֵנִ֗ים יָבִ֥ינוּ מִשְׁפָּֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: Not [the] great are wise, and [the] old understand justice.

en.L: [It is] not the great [in years who] are wise, \q nor the old [who] understand justice.
en.B: It is not the aged who are wise, \q nor the old who understand what is right.
en.R: Being old does not make people wise, \q and age alone does not teach them what is right.

decisions.choice: the great: those great in years, the aged
alternatives: the great, people of high rank
decisions.reason: The word (rabbim) usually means "many", but it can mean "great", and here, beside "the old" in the second line, it most likely means those great in years. Elihu does not say that old people are never wise, but that age alone does not make them so.

decisions.choice: not ... nor: the negative covers both lines
decisions.reason: Hebrew states the "not" once, at the start of the first line, and lets it govern the second line too.

decisions.choice: justice: what is right
decisions.reason: The word (mishpat) means justice, a right judgment. It is the question of the whole debate: whether God treats Job justly (8:3; 34:12; 40:8).

decisions.choice: being old; age alone (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the point as a general statement about age, which is what the two lines mean (m1).

source.text: לָכֵ֣ן אָ֭מַרְתִּי שִׁמְעָה־לִּ֑י אֲחַוֶּ֖ה דֵּעִ֣י אַף־אָֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore I say, listen to me; I will declare my knowledge, also I.

en.L: Therefore I say, Listen to me; \q I also will declare my knowledge.
en.B: So I say, Listen to me; \q let me also tell you what I know.
en.R: So I say, Listen to me. \q I will tell you what I think too.

decisions.choice: listen: singular
decisions.reason: The command is singular, while Elihu addresses the friends in the plural in verses 6 and 11-14. He may be turning to Job, or speaking to each listener in turn.

decisions.choice: I also: Elihu claims his turn
decisions.reason: "I also" (literally "also I") is emphatic and comes again in verse 17: the young man insists that he too has a right to speak.

decisions.choice: what I know (Balanced); what I think (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, Balanced and Readable put Elihu's "knowledge" in everyday words.

source.text: הֵ֤ן הוֹחַ֨לְתִּי לְֽדִבְרֵיכֶ֗ם אָ֭זִין עַד־תְּב֥וּנֹֽתֵיכֶ֑ם עַֽד־תַּחְקְר֥וּן מִלִּֽין׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, I waited for your words, I gave ear to your understandings, while you searched out words.

en.L: Look, I waited for your words; \q I listened to your reasonings, \q while you searched out words.
en.B: Look, I waited while you spoke; \q I listened to your arguments \q while you searched for what to say.
en.R: I waited while you talked. \q I listened to your reasons \q while you were looking for the right words.

decisions.choice: your reasonings: your insights, your arguments
decisions.reason: The word (tevunah) means understanding; in the plural it is the wise arguments the friends put forward. Elihu may use it with some irony, since in his view those arguments failed (verse 12).

decisions.choice: your: plural, the three friends
decisions.reason: Elihu now speaks to the three friends together (verses 11-14), before turning to Job in chapter 33.

decisions.choice: no "Look" (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word (hen) draws attention to what follows; Readable leaves it out as a separate word.

source.text: וְעָֽדֵיכֶ֗ם אֶתְבּ֫וֹנָ֥ן וְהִנֵּ֤ה אֵ֣ין לְאִיּ֣וֹב מוֹכִ֑יחַ עוֹנֶ֖ה אֲמָרָ֣יו מִכֶּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And to you I paid attention, and look, there [was] not for Job [one] refuting, answering his words, of you.

en.L: And I paid close attention to you, \q and look, there was no one refuting Job, \q [no one] of you answering his words.
en.B: I paid close attention to you, \q but not one of you refuted Job \q or answered his words.
en.R: I listened carefully to you. \q But none of you proved Job wrong \q or answered what he said.

decisions.choice: refuting: proving wrong in argument
decisions.reason: The verb (yakach in the causative) is a word of argument and the law court: to show that someone is in the wrong, to reprove (13:3; 13:10). The friends condemned Job (verse 3) but never proved their case.

decisions.choice: of you: not one of you
decisions.reason: "Of you" stands at the end of the verse for emphasis: none of the three succeeded.

decisions.choice: but (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Look" (hinneh) here introduces what Elihu found, which was the opposite of what he expected; Balanced and Readable say "but".

source.text: פֶּן־תֹּ֣֭אמְרוּ מָצָ֣אנוּ חָכְמָ֑ה אֵ֖ל יִדְּפֶ֣נּוּ לֹא־אִֽישׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: Lest you say, we have found wisdom; God will drive him away, not man.

en.L: So that you do not say, We have found wisdom; \q God will drive him back, not man.
en.B: Do not say, We have found wisdom: \q let God refute him, not a human being.
en.R: Do not say, We have found the wise answer: \q only God can defeat Job, not people.

decisions.choice: the friends' excuse: the quotation probably runs through the second line
alternatives: Elihu's own reply: God, not a human, will defeat him
decisions.reason: Elihu warns the friends against an excuse for their failure: they have found wisdom, namely that only God can deal with Job. Hebrew has no quotation marks, so the second line could instead be Elihu's own statement. Either way Elihu means to answer Job himself (verse 14).

decisions.choice: drive him back: defeat him, rout him
decisions.reason: The verb (nadaf) means to drive away or scatter, like a leaf or chaff blown by the wind (13:25; Psalm 1:4). Here it means to defeat Job in the argument.

decisions.choice: man: any human being
decisions.reason: The word ('ish) here means a human being as against God, not a man as against a woman.

decisions.choice: Do not say (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "lest you say" warns against saying something; Balanced and Readable put it as a plain command. Literal says "so that you do not say".

source.text: וְלֹא־עָרַ֣ךְ אֵלַ֣י מִלִּ֑ין וּ֝בְאִמְרֵיכֶ֗ם לֹ֣א אֲשִׁיבֶֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And not he has arranged against me words, and with your words not I will answer him.

en.L: And he has not arranged words against me, \q and with your words I will not answer him.
en.B: Job has not directed his words against me, \q and I will not answer him with your arguments.
en.R: Job has not argued with me, \q and I will not use your arguments to answer him.

decisions.choice: arranged: set out in order, as a case or a battle line
decisions.reason: The verb ('arakh) is used for drawing up an army in order and for laying out a legal case (13:18; 23:4; 33:5). Job's case was set against the friends and against God, not against Elihu.

decisions.choice: with your words: Elihu promises a fresh answer
decisions.reason: Because he has not been part of the quarrel, Elihu claims he can answer Job without repeating the friends' arguments. Readers can judge how far his speeches do so.

decisions.choice: Job (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Job, since "he" follows a verse that ends with God.

source.text: חַ֭תּוּ לֹא־עָ֣נוּ ע֑וֹד הֶעְתִּ֖יקוּ מֵהֶ֣ם מִלִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: They are dismayed, not they answer again; they have moved from them words.

en.L: They are dismayed; they answer no more; \q words have moved away from them.
en.B: They are dismayed and answer no more; \q they have run out of words.
en.R: They are upset and have no more answers. \q They have nothing left to say.

decisions.choice: they: Elihu now speaks about the friends, not to them
decisions.reason: In verses 15-16 the friends are "they", where in verses 11-14 they were "you". Elihu seems to turn aside, to Job or to those listening, and describe the friends' silence.

decisions.choice: words have moved away from them: they have nothing left to say
alternatives: they have removed words from themselves
decisions.reason: The verb ('ataq) means to move on or move away (9:5; 14:18). The words have left them: they are speechless.

decisions.choice: run out of words (Balanced); nothing left to say (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say in plain English what the picture means (m2).

source.text: וְ֭הוֹחַלְתִּי כִּי־לֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ כִּ֥י עָ֝מְד֗וּ לֹא־עָ֥נוּ עֽוֹד׃

records.literal_gloss: And shall I wait, because not they speak, because they stand, not they answer again?

en.L: And shall I wait because they do not speak, \q because they stand [there and] answer no more?
en.B: Must I wait because they do not speak, \q because they stand there and answer no more?
en.R: Should I keep waiting just because they are silent, \q standing there with no answer?

decisions.choice: a question: shall I go on waiting?
alternatives: a statement: I have waited, but they do not speak
decisions.reason: The verb form can be read as a statement ("and I waited") or, as here, as a question that expects the answer no. The question fits verse 17, where Elihu decides to speak.

decisions.choice: stand: stand still, stop
decisions.reason: "To stand" here means to stand still and do nothing (Joshua 10:13, of the sun), as people do when they have nothing more to say.

source.text: אַעֲנֶ֣ה אַף־אֲנִ֣י חֶלְקִ֑י אֲחַוֶּ֖ה דֵעִ֣י אַף־אָֽנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: I will answer, also I, my part; I will declare my knowledge, also I.

en.L: I also will answer my part; \q I also will declare my knowledge.
en.B: I too will give my answer; \q I too will tell what I know.
en.R: Now it is my turn to answer. \q I will tell you what I think.

decisions.choice: my part: my share of the answer
decisions.reason: The word (cheleq) is a share or portion. Elihu claims his part in the debate, his turn to answer.

decisions.choice: I also ... I also: emphatic repetition
decisions.reason: Elihu says "also I" twice in one verse, as in verse 10: he insists on his right to be heard.

decisions.choice: it is my turn (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "my part" means here (m1) and lets the sentence carry the emphasis of "I also".

source.text: כִּ֭י מָלֵ֣תִי מִלִּ֑ים הֱ֝צִיקַ֗תְנִי ר֣וּחַ בִּטְנִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: For I am full of words; it constrains me, [the] spirit of my belly.

en.L: For I am full of words; \q the spirit of my belly presses me.
en.B: For I am full of words; \q the spirit within me drives me on.
en.R: I am full of words. \q My spirit is pushing me to speak.

decisions.choice: the spirit: the inner breath and urge, given by God
decisions.reason: The word (ruach) means wind, breath or spirit. Here it is the spirit in Elihu that he has said comes from God (verse 8), now pressing to get out, like the wind in the wineskins of verse 19. "Spirit" keeps the link with verse 8.

decisions.choice: belly: the inner self
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the belly is the seat of thought and feeling, the innermost part of a person (15:35; Proverbs 18:8; 20:27). It returns in verse 19.

decisions.choice: presses me: constrains, urges me on
decisions.reason: The verb (tsuq) means to press hard or put under pressure (Judges 14:17; 16:16).

decisions.choice: within me (Balanced); my spirit (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Belly" as the inner self is not natural English (m2); Balanced says "within me", Readable "my spirit". Literal keeps the picture.

source.text: הִנֵּֽה־בִטְנִ֗י כְּיַ֥יִן לֹא־יִפָּתֵ֑חַ כְּאֹב֥וֹת חֲ֝דָשִׁ֗ים יִבָּקֵֽעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, my belly [is] like wine not opened; like new wineskins it will burst.

en.L: Look, my belly [is] like wine [that] is not opened; \q like new wineskins it is about to burst.
en.B: Look, inside I am like wine with no vent; \q like new wineskins, I am ready to burst.
en.R: Inside, I am like wine sealed up with no way for the air to escape. \q Like new wineskins, I am ready to burst.

decisions.choice: wine not opened, wineskins about to burst: fermenting wine in a sealed skin
decisions.reason: Wine was stored in skins. As new wine ferments, its gas swells the skin, and if it has no vent the skin splits (Matthew 9:17). Elihu's words, held back for so long, press to come out in the same way.

decisions.choice: new wineskins: perhaps "skins of new wine"
decisions.reason: New skins stretch more easily than old ones, so it is surprising that they should burst. The phrase may mean skins holding new wine, still fermenting; the image is the same either way: a container about to give way.

decisions.choice: inside I am (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 18, Balanced and Readable say "inside" for the belly as the inner self.

source.text: אֲדַבְּרָ֥ה וְיִֽרְוַֽח־לִ֑י אֶפְתַּ֖ח שְׂפָתַ֣י וְאֶֽעֱנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Let me speak, and it may be relief to me; let me open my lips and answer.

en.L: Let me speak, so that it may be relief to me; \q let me open my lips and answer.
en.B: I must speak and find relief; \q I must open my lips and answer.
en.R: I must speak so that I can feel better. \q I must open my mouth and answer.

decisions.choice: relief: room to breathe
decisions.reason: The verb (ravach) means to be spacious, to have room, and so to find relief (1 Samuel 16:23). It sounds like the word for spirit or wind (ruach) in verse 18: once the pent-up wind is let out, Elihu can breathe again.

decisions.choice: I must (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The verbs express Elihu's resolve; "I must" carries their urgency after verses 18-19.

source.text: אַל־נָ֭א אֶשָּׂ֣א פְנֵי־אִ֑ישׁ וְאֶל־אָ֝דָ֗ם לֹ֣א אֲכַנֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Not please let me lift up [the] face of anyone, and to a human not I will give flattering titles.

en.L: Let me not lift up the face of anyone, \q and to any human I will not give flattering titles.
en.B: I will not take anyone's side, \q nor flatter any human being.
en.R: I will not favor anyone, \q and I will not use fancy titles to flatter anyone.

decisions.choice: lift up the face of: show favor, take sides
decisions.reason: To "lift someone's face" is to accept or favor them, and in a dispute to be partial (Leviticus 19:15; Job 13:8, 10). Elihu promises to judge the case fairly, without deference to the older men or to Job.

decisions.choice: give flattering titles: address with honorific names
decisions.reason: The verb (kanah) means to give someone a title or a name of honor (Isaiah 44:5; 45:4). Elihu will not use the polite flattery that a young man might owe his elders.

decisions.choice: take anyone's side (Balanced); favor (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m1); Literal keeps the picture.

source.text: כִּ֤י לֹ֣א יָדַ֣עְתִּי אֲכַנֶּ֑ה כִּ֝מְעַ֗ט יִשָּׂאֵ֥נִי עֹשֵֽׂנִי׃

records.literal_gloss: For not I know [how] to give flattering titles; in a little would carry me away my Maker.

en.L: For I do not know [how] to flatter; \q [else] in a little [while] my Maker would carry me away.
en.B: For I do not know how to flatter; \q if I did, my Maker would soon carry me away.
en.R: I do not know how to flatter people. \q If I did, God who made me would soon put an end to me.

decisions.choice: [else]: an unstated condition
decisions.reason: The second line leaves its condition unspoken: if Elihu were to flatter, God would soon remove him. Hebrew often lets the context supply such an "if".

decisions.choice: carry me away: remove, sweep away in judgment
decisions.reason: The verb (nasa') means to lift and carry off; used of the wind carrying away the wicked (27:21), it means sudden death or ruin.

decisions.choice: my Maker: God
decisions.reason: Elihu calls God his Maker (35:10; 36:3), as Eliphaz did (4:17). The one who made him will hold him to account for what he says.

decisions.choice: God who made me would soon put an end to me (Readable)
alternatives: my Maker would carry me away
decisions.reason: Readable names God and says plainly what "carry me away" means (m2).
